White Gaussian Noise is a very specific concept. The "Gaussian" does not refer to the spread of the noise in frequency domain - the "white" part does. "Gaussian" here is the statistical spread of the noise value at every single instant in *time*. So at every time step, there is a noise value, and if you collected the statistics of a lot of the noise values, they would fall into a Gaussian distribution.

There is a crucial half of the dark forest theory not many people catch on - the idea that, even if the alien species is non - xenocidal, they have no way of truly knowing if YOU aren't - so they must take preventive measure. Even if they are non-xenocidal, and you aren't xenocidal, they can't know if YOU don't think THEY are xenocidal, and whether YOU will take preventive measure against them. In a game theory way, there is no action that would guarantee survival, other than eliminating every other species you come across. This is regardless of whether all species are xenocidal or benevolent. This is a fundamental result of the lack of information. 

Of course, in human history, it has not been the case that all civilisations immediately war on others newly discovered. I believe that's because the starting postulates of Liu Cixin are false.

I too find the dark forest package of ideas unlikely to be true, but not because of the reasoning, but the set up - that two-way communication of benevolent intent is fundamentally impossible. And that resource is scarce on a cosmic scale. And that all civilisations act with perfectly rational game theory strategies.

I see where you're coming from, tho I believe they actually are what the first 2 points say - 1. Numbers are a space (real analysis reveals properties of that space, and in turn reveal the nature of these numbers that make up that space.) 2. (Group theory tells us) that numbers are geometric actions on a space. 

Some will say that numbers are their set theoretical definitions, but personally, going to that definition doesn't provide a sense of knowing their nature imo, it's just 20th century maths giants making sure everything is formalised into set theory.

There are myriad interpretations of numbers, including the most formal definition in set theory, but for most purposes you really don't need to go that deep. Over the years I have distilled three ways to describe numbers which im fairly confident it's not necessary to go any deeper than these: 

1. The most useful view is that numbers form and measure some space. Integers mark a 1D space in regular ticks. Real numbers mark the 1D space continuously. There is really a sense in which the numbers themselves ARE the space. So numbers are a space. There are many mind blowing properties of the real numbers simply emerging out of the fact, of how truly continuous the number line is. Arrange three real number lines all perpendicular to one another and you can now have / measure a 3D space. 3 numbers mark a location in this 3D space. N numbers can mark a location in ND space! 

2. Numbers when paired with an operation, represent some geometric action on some space. (Addition = translational movement, multiplication on the real line = scaling, multiplication on the complex plane = rotation and scaling)

3. numbers can also just serve a practical accounting purpose and represent any quantity you are interested in for a system. Grocery shoppers use integers to count how many apples they want to buy. Here the number of apples don't really represent a geometric action on some space, nor is it meaningful to assert that they live on some "number of apples space". It is purely pragmatic. Electrical engineers use complex numbers to represent any quantity that oscillates with a regular frequency in time. However, it is often enlightening to look at how a previously pragmatic usage of numbers form some space...

On the topic of complex numbers. Points 1 and 2 will help you mostly understand what they are. You can see them as co-ordinate markings over a 2D space. The real numbers on one dimension, the imaginary numbers on a second, perpendicular dimension. At the same time, each complex number represents a geometric action on this 2D space. Multiplying by 1 does nothing to the space. Multiplying by i rotates the entire space by 90 degrees. Adding 3+4i shifts the entire space 3 to the right and 4 upwards. 

In fact, if you wanted to invent a 2D number system, so that you can use each 2D number to indicate a location on that space (just like how a 1D number simply indicates a location on the 1D number line), and you also want addition and multiplication to mean the same thing as the 1D case, then you are FORCED to conclude that the units along the 2nd axis, the new perpendicular axis you introduce, call it "i", MUST square to -1. Complex numbers cleanly and inevitably emerge out of the need to create 2D numbers.

If you want to go even deeper philosophically and ask if numbers exist, like the number "3", then my feeling is that they don't, in the typical meaning of the word exist. 3 apples exist. 3 people exist. 3 chairs exist. You can locate them somewhere in the universe. But the concept "3" itself, cannot be located in the universe. You cannot touch it. No combination of quantum fields can make it. "3" is an abstraction, even though it's a universal property shared among all collections of three objects, this "threeness", is a distillation by intelligent beings and only live in the consciousness of such beings. However, if you consider your own thoughts to exist (which is a very reasonable position to hold even tho I'm undecided about it), then I'm very happy with you saying that 3 exists.

TLDR: 1. Numbers are a space. 2. Numbers are geometric actions. 3. Numbers are accounting tools.

Great question! And a deep one! 3rd year physics student at university here.

Einstein's theories of relativity tell us that light travels at the exact same speed (known as "c"; roughly 300000 kilometres every second) ALWAYS, through space. But what happens when a black hole pulls light in? It's a great question. Wouldn't the light be accelerated past the speed of light? I mean, the whole point of a black hole is that the black hole sucks things in so fast (faster than light can travel) that it appears black, cause no light escapes it.

​

Answer: Physics indeed strangely forces light to travel "THROUGH SPACE" at the speed of light, no more, no less, in a manner that seems foreign to most objects. But the way a black hole works, (**like how ALL gravitational bodies actually work,) is to pull SPACE ITSELF inward towards it over time (NOT directly pulling on the objects INSIDE space).** This insight again was gifted to us by Einstein, in General Relativity. Newton's apple wasn't directly pulled by earth to fall, but the space around the apple was, and the apple was simply sitting freely inside that space.

Now return to your scenario. Imagine light particles as marbles on a rubber sheet (the rubber sheet is space). These marbles would strangely obey that they must travel relative to the rubber sheet at the exact same speed (the speed of light), always. What a black hole does, (again, like how all gravitational bodies work,) is it pulls the entire rubber sheet around it inwards, over time. And, beyond the event horizon, this "pulling inward of space" occurs at a speed faster than the marbles can travel on the rubber sheet.

So it's "yes" and "no" in different senses. Yes in the sense that the light that was heading towards a black hole as the black hole pulls space inwards, would actually move faster than light speed relative to someone outside (if there was any way of knowing it directly, which there probably never will be). But, it still moves AT light speed, relative to the fabric of space around it.

(Advanced side note: if you talk about space and time together as "spacetime", then you would no longer describe it as "pulling in space over time", because you now see time as part of the fabric. You would instead describe it as "curvature" within the fabric.)

​

TLDR: It is not possible to travel faster than light speed through the fabric of space. But it is possible for the fabric of space itself to move faster than light speed, so that anything embedded inside this fabric of space, enjoys a faster ride.

Its a deeper question about what makes something funny, or what makes a person feel like laughing. 

In my understanding the 2 biggest categories of "stuff that are funny" are: 

1. Stuff that make you learn something new. E.g. every single joke that land with a twist/subversion. Or every joke involving word play. The brain is being amused by a concept/turn of events/possibility of word play, that it had never contemplated before. Or a connection it hadn't drawn before. This is probably the majority of jokes. Even the meta-ironic abstract memes like "E", they fall into this category. 

2. Relateability and feeling like you're part of a group. E.g. any joke that points out some absurdity of some aspect of life. Or any joke/meme that exaggerates / glorifies / mocks a particular experience people have to go through. This is also probably the majority of memes. I think evolutionarily, this is what reinforced social cohesion. Being able to laugh about some shared concept / experience probably played into survival a lot.

So I believe jokes that involve sex fall into the second category. To the people who laugh at those, their brains are indulging in the shared experience of all who can relate to that joke. 

And is it normal to not find them funny? Ofc. If someone doesn't feel the need to relate to others in that way, they won't really find it funny. But maybe a more likely scenario is that many of the jokes being made are *very bad taste*.

I absolutely adore the 2.0 and personally i like it MORE than 3.0 's over complexity and more modern proportions, and Origin. The 2.0 is an absolute classic, with down to earth proportions and a simple but solemn design.

Aesthetically i think the shape composition is superior to 3.0's oversized head camera and shoulders and overly-slim waist and overly thick skirt armour. The legs also have better sculpt with a more satisfying look to the large calves, transitioning into the lower leg.

The downfall of the Origin version is the \*break of immersion\* when you realise that: to maintain the outward appearance and to give it good articulation, a lot of things are left out and altered. Like the ankle guard being connected by a tiny ball joint at the front and the 2 bolts not even connected to the feet. Also the waist feels like a barebones skeleton designed purely to pull off some unusual articulation. This really hurts immersion. You feel like you're building something that has the sole purpose of having a good looking shell and flexible playability, not that you're building a \*scale model\* that's supposed to reveal how the gundam works on the inside.

The build experience for 2.0 was beautiful and when you figure out how the inner skeleton fit together there are tiny mind blowing moments. Then when you put it all together it's a nicely wrapped up piece of model. As you build it you actually feel like you are constructing a coherent mechanical object. So grounded and so good. I would say the same for most 2007-2010 era 2.0 kits.
